semin-durr:1-1.t:
His saying: {القارعة مَا القارعة}: like His saying {الحاقة مَا الحآقة} [al-Ḥāqqa: 12] and like His saying {وَأَصْحَابُ اليمين مَآ أَصْحَابُ اليمين} [al-Wāqiʿa: 27]; both have been treated earlier. You have already learned from what Makkī transmitted that it is permissible to put «القارعة» in the nominative by an implied verb that governs «يومَ» in the accusative. It was also said that the meaning of the sentence is one of warning (taḥdhīr). Al-Zajjāj said: "The Arabs warn and urge (tughrī) with the nominative as with the accusative." And he recited:
4631 - لَجَديرون بالوفاءِ إذا ق ... لَ أخو النجدةِ السِّلاحُ السِّلاحُ
(They are indeed fit for loyalty when the man of valour says: "Arms! Arms!")
I say: this was already treated in His saying {نَاقَةَ الله} [al-Shams: 13], for the one who read it in the nominative. And what shows this is the reading of ʿĪsā, {القارعةَ ما القارعةَ} in the accusative, by an implied verb, that is, "beware of the Striking Calamity", with «ما» redundant (zāʾida). The second «القارعة» is an emphasis (tawkīd) of the first, a verbal emphasis (tawkīd lafẓī).

semin-durr:4-4.t:
His saying: {يَوْمَ يَكُونُ}: there are several views on what governs it. The first: an implied verb which «القارعةُ» indicates, that is, "it strikes them on the day when it comes"; it was also said that the implied form is "the Striking Calamity comes on the day". The second: that it is an implied «اذْكُرْ» ("remember"), so that it is a direct object (mafʿūl bihi) and not an adverbial (ẓarf). The third: that it is «القارعة»; Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Abū l-Baqāʾ and Makkī said so. Al-Shaykh said: "If Ibn ʿAṭiyya meant the first word, that is not permissible, because of the separation between the governor, which is within the ṣila (relative clause) of the definite article al-, and the governed word by a foreign element, namely the khabar. And if he made «القارعة» a proper name for the Resurrection, it does not govern either. And if he meant the second and the third, the meaning of adverbial time does not fit with it." The fourth: that it is an implied verb that puts the first «القارعةُ» in the nominative, as if it had been said: "the Striking Calamity comes on the day when it happens"; Makkī said so. On this, what lies between would be a parenthetical clause (iʿtirāḍ), which is very far-fetched and out of tune with the construction of the sentence. Zayd ibn ʿAlī read «يومُ» in the nominative, as the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ (subject), that is: "its time is the day when it happens".
His saying: {كالفراش}: it may be the khabar of the incomplete verb (kāna al-nāqiṣa), and it may be a ḥāl (circumstantial) from the agent of the complete verb (kāna al-tāmma), that is, "they will be found and gathered in the likeness of moths (al-farāsh)". It is a well-known flying creature. It was also said: it is the gnats (al-hamaj) among mosquitoes, locusts and the like; the proverb of giddiness and recklessness is struck with it. One says: "lighter-witted than a moth", and the following was recited:
4632 - فَراشَةُ الحُلْمِ فِرْعَوْنُ العذابِ وإنْ ... يُطْلَبُ نَداه فكَلْبٌ دونَه كَلْبُ
(A moth in forbearance, a Pharaoh in punishment; and if his generosity is sought, a dog, and a dog behind him.)
And another said:
4633 - وقد كانَ أقوامٌ رَدَدْتُ قلوبَهُمْ ... عليهم وكانوا كالفَراشِ من الجهلِ
(There were people whose hearts I restored to them, and they were like moths in ignorance.)
Al-farāsha is also the little water in a vessel, and "the farāsha of the lock" is so called from its resemblance to the moth. In likening people to moths there are various kinds of emphasis (mubālagha), among them: the giddiness that afflicts them, their spreading over the earth, their mounting one another, their great number, weakness and abasement, their coming without going away, their heading for the caller from every direction, and their flying toward the fire. Jarīr said:
4634 - إنَّ الفرزدقَ ما عَلِمْتَ وقومَه ... مثلُ الفَراشِ غَشِيْنَ نارَ المُصْطَلي
(Al-Farazdaq, as you know, and his people are like moths that have flocked to the fire of the one warming himself.)
And al-ʿihn was treated under Saʾala.

semin-durr:9-9.t:
His saying: {فَأُمُّهُ هَاوِيَةٌ}: that is, perishing (hālika). This is a proverb. They say of one who perishes: "his mother has fallen" (hawat ummuhu), because when he perishes his mother falls in bereavement and grief. On this is the saying of the poet:
463 - 5- هَوَتْ أمُّه ما يَبْعَثُ الصبحُ غادياً ... وماذا يَرُدُّ الليلُ حين يَؤُوْبُ
(His mother is bereaved! What does the morning send forth as it goes out, and what does the night bring back when it returns!)
[Translator's note: the verse number is printed in the source as «463 - 5-», evidently 4635, following 4634 in the preceding entry.]
Ṭalḥa read «فإمُّه» with kasra on the hamza. Ibn Khālawayh transmitted from Ibn Durayd that it is a dialect form. The grammarians do not allow this except when a kasra or a yāʾ precedes it. The verification of this was given in Sūrat al-Nisāʾ, together with the disagreement of the readers on it.

semin-durr:10-10.t: His saying: {مَا هِيَهْ}: a mubtadaʾ and khabar standing in the place of the two objects of «أَدْراك»; this is a case of suspension (taʿlīq). «هي» is a pronoun referring to al-hāwiya, if al-hāwiya is, as has been said, a name for one of the levels (darakāt) of the Fire; otherwise it refers to the calamity (al-dāhiya) understood from al-hāwiya. Ḥamza dropped the hāʾ of pause (hāʾ al-sakta) in running speech. The verification of this was given in al-Ḥāqqa. «نارٌ» is the khabar of an implied mubtadaʾ, that is: "it is a fire".
